reviewer: R9 – Associate Editor of Analytica Chimica Acta
summary: The submission applies the deterministic-equivalent (random-matrix) risk of ridge regression to the learning curves of 38 public NIR/MIR/VisNIR calibration tasks. It proposes regularisation-path matching (RPM) to forecast calibration error from small pilot sets and benchmarks RPM against curve-fitting extrapolation (IPL3 etc.), a no-improvement rule (FLAT) and a post-hoc transferred-slope rule (SLOPE-T). The work is careful about leakage, reproducible and unusually candid about negative results. As an ACA editor, though, I see a central problem with how it is framed. The proposed method (RPM) beats only the curve-fitting extrapolations. It is not better than simply reporting the pilot's own cross-validated error: overall Holm p = 0.148, RPM worse on 23/38 tasks. On the 23 soil tasks it is significantly worse than FLAT (recomputed Wilcoxon p = 0.0024), and it is also worse than FLAT at n0 = 200 (0.164 vs 0.139). It is the worst non-FLAT method on the pre-registered sample-size decision endpoint (4.7%/2.0%). The practical recommendation (pilot CV error plus about 8.3% RMSE reduction per doubling) is a post-hoc rule. It is itself a power-law extrapolation, which contradicts the Significance statement that power-law extrapolation 'should be abandoned'. Its slope is dominated by soil libraries: the non-soil median is about 17.7% per doubling. Its claimed explanation (noise floor as the 'dominant' driver of slope) is confounded with the calibration-size range over which slopes were fitted. The scientific core is worth publishing in ACA as a fundamental chemometric study of what learning curves can and cannot tell an analyst, but not as a new forecasting method that is better than current practice. The package also has editorial and technical defects that would trigger an immediate technical return: Fig. 1 missing and numbering starting at Fig. 2, four figures never cited, wrong supplementary cross-references, three silently truncated supplementary tables, raw variable names and duplicated sentences in the text, internal workflow jargon, no graphical abstract, and author and declaration placeholders. I would send it for review only after these are fixed and the paper is reframed.
strengths: Addresses a real and general analytical-chemistry planning problem (how many reference analyses to buy), relevant to every quantitative NIR/MIR application.

Unusually rigorous leakage control (replicate averaging, group-disjoint splits, exact LOGO, unlabelled spectra from the pool only; Supplementary Note 2) and a large, multi-domain benchmark (2,640 pilots, 38 tasks, 9 sources).

The critique of curve-shape extrapolation is robust: IPL3 is worse than RPM on 35/38 tasks, and in my source-level re-aggregation of raw_results.csv IPL3 was worse in all 9 data sources (sign test p = 0.004). EXP3/LOG2/DF-OLS fail dramatically (Table 2).

Negative results (RPM-T failure, no method able to forecast the required sample size, under-covering bootstrap bands) are reported rather than hidden, and the identifiability argument (Section 2.4, 4.4) gives a principled explanation.
Full reproducibility: public data, deterministic seeds, a single script regenerating all numbers, tables and figures.

issues.title: The proposed method shows no advantage over the trivial no-improvement rule; the paper is framed as a methods advance it does not deliver (main desk-rejection risk under ACA scope)
issues.description: ACA's aims and scope require new methodology to show clear superiority over existing alternatives in some important respect, and to compare with previously reported methods. RPM is superior only to the curve-fitting extrapolations (IPL3, IPL2, EXP3, LOG2, DF-OLS). It is not superior to the simplest possible alternative, reporting the pilot's own CV error (FLAT). FLAT has a mean error of 0.266 vs 0.284 for RPM, Holm p = 0.148, and RPM is worse on 23/38 tasks. RPM is also significantly worse than the post-hoc SLOPE-T (Holm p = 0.031). In the dominant application domain, the 23 soil tasks, RPM is significantly worse than FLAT (task means 0.250 vs 0.211; Table S30). At the largest pilot size RPM (0.164) is worse than both FLAT (0.139) and the classical DF-OLS formula (0.140) (Table S7). On the pre-registered decision endpoint (RQ3) RPM is correct in only 4.7%/2.0% of pilots, vs 25.1%/9.2% for IPL3 and 29.5%/21.1% for SLOPE-T (Section 4.5). In the post-hoc gain analysis RPM's predicted gain is no more accurate than predicting no gain (0.231 vs 0.245, Holm p = 1.000). The pre-registered RQ2 explicitly asked whether RPM beats 'learning-curve extrapolation and simple rules' (Supplementary Note 1). The second half is not supported, and RQ3 is not supported. Yet the Abstract, Highlights and cover letter present RPM as the success story ('reduced the error to 0.284 (better on 35 of 38 tasks; p < 0.0001)'), and recommendation (vi) of Section 4.10 calls RPM-w 'far more reliable than curve-shape extrapolation'. An ACA editor or referee will read this as: the new method loses to doing nothing. That is grounds for desk rejection unless the paper is reframed around its genuine contribution, an analysis of what pilot-based learning-curve forecasts can and cannot achieve.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md Abstract (Results); Section 4.3 Table 2 (RPM 0.284; FLAT 0.266, Δ -0.021, Holm p 0.1485, RPM better/worse 15/23; SLOPE-T 0.251, Holm p 0.0310); Section 4.5 decision metric; Section 4.10 (vi). manuscript/build/supplementary_full.md Table S7 (n0 = 200: RPM 0.164, FLAT 0.139, DFOLS 0.140); Table S30 (soil: RPM 0.250, FLAT 0.211); Table S22/S23 (gain). Supplementary Note 1 RQ2 ('more accurately than learning-curve extrapolation and simple rules') and RQ3. My recomputation from results/raw_results.csv (per-task mean abs_err): soil tasks, FLAT better than RPM on 17/23, Wilcoxon p = 0.0024. Non-soil, RPM better than FLAT on 9/15, p = 0.68. Aims and scope (Elsevier journal page): new methods must show 'clear superiority over existing alternatives in some important respect'.
issues.corrective_action: Reframe the paper. The title, abstract, highlights and cover letter should present the contribution as a fundamental analysis of calibration learning curves and of the limits of pilot-based forecasting: the theory, the identifiability limit, the failure of curve-shape extrapolation, and the adequacy of the pilot CV error. They should not present RPM as a superior forecaster. State explicitly in the Abstract that the pre-registered hypothesis that RPM would beat simple rules (RQ2) and support better sample-size decisions (RQ3) was not supported. Report the family-stratified paired tests, including RPM vs FLAT on soil (significantly worse) and at n0 = 200, in the main text. Either delete recommendation (vi) or restate it as 'RPM-w is no more accurate than the pilot's CV error but, unlike curve fitting, is not optimistic'. Specify a concrete situation in which RPM adds value over FLAT (if any), or state that none was found.

issues.title: The recommended planning rule (SLOPE-T) is itself a power-law extrapolation, contradicting the headline 'power-law extrapolation should be abandoned'
issues.description: SLOPE-T forecasts log RMSE(n) = log RMSE_CV(n0) + s·log2(n/n0), with s about -0.086. That is exactly a pure power law, RMSE ∝ n^(s/ln2) ≈ n^-0.12, anchored at the pilot CV error with an exponent transferred from other data sets. The Significance paragraph ('Power-law extrapolation from small pilot sets should be abandoned'), Highlight 4, the cover letter and recommendation (i) of Section 4.10 therefore contradict the paper's own recommendation (ii). What the data show is narrower: fitting the curve shape to sub-samples of a small pilot (IPL2/IPL3/EXP3/LOG2) is unreliable. Using a power law with an externally fixed exponent is what the authors recommend. Referees from the chemometrics community will spot this immediately.
issues.evidence: code/experiments/analysis.py, add_slope_transfer(): base['fc_logrmse'] = base.pilot_cv_logrmse + base.task.map(loso) * np.log2(base.n / base.n0). manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md Abstract (Significance); Section 4.10 (i) vs (ii); manuscript/Highlights.pdf bullet 4; manuscript/cover_letter.pdf paragraph 3.
issues.corrective_action: Rephrase all such statements as 'fitting a learning-curve shape to sub-samples of a small pilot should be abandoned'. Say explicitly that SLOPE-T is a power law with a transferred exponent and that the failure of IPL2/IPL3 lies in estimating the exponent and asymptote from the pilot, not in the functional form. Revise Highlight 4 accordingly.

issues.title: The claim that learning-curve slopes are 'governed mainly by the irreducible-noise fraction' is confounded by the calibration-size range over which slopes were fitted
issues.description: Slopes per doubling were fitted by regressing log RMSE on log2 n over each task's whole ground-truth curve. Those curves span very different ranges: only two points (n = 50, 100) for the 7 CGL and Tecator tasks, 50–200 for Diesel, and 50–6400 for KSSL. Because curves flatten as they approach the noise floor, tasks with long curves (large pools) must have shallower average slopes, whatever the noise fraction. The authors' own Table S4 shows that pool size is at least as strong a correlate of slope as the noise fraction (Spearman ρ = 0.624 vs 0.590), and the two descriptors are themselves correlated. The abstract and Section 4.2 nevertheless call the noise fraction 'the dominant term' and draw the conclusion that 'a learning curve cannot be read from its first points'.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/supplementary_full.md Table S4 (n_pool ρ = 0.624, p = 2.8e-5; noise_frac ρ = 0.590, p = 9.6e-5); Table S1 / Table 1 'Max. n (truth)' (100 to 6,400). results/slope_per_doubling.csv and results/alignment_exponents.csv, recomputed: Spearman(noise_frac, n_pool) = 0.55 (p = 0.0004). Partial rank correlation of slope with noise fraction controlling for n_pool = 0.38 (p = 0.019); with n_pool controlling for noise = 0.45 (p = 0.005). results/raw/truth_*.npz: 7 tasks have only 2 truth points. manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md Abstract; Section 4.2 paragraph 3.
issues.corrective_action: Recompute slopes over a common calibration-size window that all eligible tasks share (e.g. n = 50–200 or 100–400), or as local slopes at matched n. Repeat the regression with log(max n) or n_pool as a covariate. Report the theory-predicted local slope at matched n as a function of noise fraction. Tone down 'dominant' unless the adjusted analysis supports it.

issues.title: The '8.3% per doubling' planning rule and the calibrated bands are driven by soil libraries and are not representative of the pharmaceutical, food, fuel and mixture applications that dominate ACA's readership
issues.description: 23 of the 38 tasks, and 4 of the 9 sources, are OSSL soil libraries. As a result, every leave-one-source-out slope prior used by SLOPE-T lies in the narrow band -0.084 to -0.099, even for tasks whose true slope is -0.2 to -0.5. For the 15 non-soil tasks the median slope is -0.195 (about 17.7% RMSE reduction per doubling), more than twice the soil value (-0.081, 7.8%). The range runs from +0.117 (Diesel:total) to -0.528 (CGL:moisture). On these non-soil tasks SLOPE-T (0.316) is not distinguishable from RPM (0.336), being worse than RPM on 7/15 tasks. The practical recommendation (Section 4.10 ii-iii; Abstract 'Significance'; Conclusions) is stated as a general rule for NIR/MIR calibration. The 'honest 80% band' width of about 1.77 is calibrated on the same 38 tasks. The authors themselves state in Limitations item 3 that the rule needs prospective validation, and that validation is missing.
issues.evidence: results/slope_per_doubling.csv (slope_loso_prior range -0.0992 to -0.0844; recomputed medians: soil -0.081, non-soil -0.195). manuscript/build/supplementary_full.md Table S5 (CGL median -0.415, Tecator -0.195, Diesel -0.121 [-0.428, +0.117]). Recomputed from results/raw_results.csv: non-soil task means SLOPE-T 0.316, RPM 0.336, FLAT 0.351, IPL3 0.435. SLOPE-T worse than RPM on 7/15 (Wilcoxon p = 0.45). manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md Section 4.10 (ii)-(iii); Section 5 item 3; Table 1.
issues.corrective_action: Report slopes and SLOPE-T performance separately for soil and non-soil applications in the main text, and qualify the rule as soil-library specific unless external validation supports it. Give domain-specific slope priors and bands, or state that a prior must come from comparable calibrations. Validate SLOPE-T, FLAT, RPM-w and the LOSO-conformal bands on held-out non-soil data sets that were not used to derive the slope prior.
issues.proposed_experiment: External validation on at least 3–5 additional public non-soil NIR/MIR calibration data sets with at least 1,000 samples, so that curves extend to 8–16× extrapolation (e.g. large public grain/feed, milk/dairy, fruit or pharmaceutical NIR data sets). Run the identical pilot protocol, and freeze the slope prior and conformal quantiles from the current 38 tasks before running it. Report forecast error, bias and band coverage.

issues.title: Tasks are treated as independent units although they are clustered in 9 sources (several properties measured on the same spectra); several 'significant' differences do not survive source-level analysis
issues.description: All paired Wilcoxon tests use the 38 tasks as independent observations. However, up to 6 tasks share identical spectra and pilot draws: 4 properties per OSSL library, 6 Diesel properties, 4 CGL constituents, 3 Tecator properties. Soil libraries contribute 23 tasks. The IPL3 result is robust to this clustering. In my source-level re-aggregation, though, RPM-w is better than RPM in only 5 of 9 sources (sign test p = 1.0, Wilcoxon p = 0.65), although the manuscript reports Holm p = 0.023. SLOPE-T is better than RPM in 7 of 9 sources (sign test p = 0.18), compared with the reported Holm p = 0.031. Claims such as 'RPM-w ... the paired difference to RPM was significant' and 'SLOPE-T ... significantly better than the pre-registered RPM' therefore rest on pseudo-replication. Referees with a statistics background will raise this.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md Section 3.7 ('The task is the unit of analysis'); Section 4.3 (RPM-w Holm p = 0.023; SLOPE-T Holm p = 0.031); Table 2. results/statistics.json ('ridge' block). Recomputed from results/raw_results.csv with sources ICRAF, KSSL, AfSIS1, Neospectra, Mango, Diesel, Tablets, Tecator, CGL: IPL3 worse than RPM in 9/9 sources (p = 0.004); RPM-w vs RPM 5/4 (Wilcoxon p = 0.65); SLOPE-T better than RPM in 7/9 (Wilcoxon p = 0.039, sign test p = 0.18); FLAT better than RPM in 7/9 (Wilcoxon p = 0.13).
issues.corrective_action: Add a source-level (cluster) analysis as the primary or a co-primary inference: source-level paired tests, a cluster bootstrap over sources, or a mixed model with a random source effect. Report which conclusions survive, and revise the wording for RPM-w and SLOPE-T accordingly.

issues.title: Manuscript assembly defects: missing Fig. 1, uncited figures, wrong supplementary cross-references, silently truncated supplementary tables, raw code variable names and duplicated text
issues.description: Each defect alone is minor, but together they would cause an immediate technical return at ACA and signal an unreviewed, machine-assembled manuscript. (a) The main text starts at Fig. 2. A workflow figure (figures/Fig1_workflow.png) exists but is not included, so the figures are numbered 2–10. (b) Figs. 7, 8, 9 and 10 are never cited in the text, only captioned. (c) Section 4.7 cites the simulation as 'Supplementary Tables S21–S22'. S21 is the decision metric and S22 the gain analysis; the simulation tables are S26–S27. (d) The supplementary build truncates every table at 60 rows (build_supplementary.py md_table(maxrows=60)). Table S2 (theory validity, cited for 'all 38 tasks') shows only 30 tasks, with Neospectra, Tablets and Tecator missing. Table S16 shows 60 of 264 rows and Table S26 60 of 108 rows, with no indication of truncation. (e) Section 4.9 prints code identifiers and 'p = 0.000': 'eigen_decay_exponent ρ = -0.06 (p = 0.701); theory_fit_err ρ = +0.57 (p = 0.000); noise_frac ...; n_pool ...'. (f) Auto-generated duplications and garbles: Section 4.5 '(pilots of 50–200 samples): For pilots of 50–200 samples the mean task error ...'; Section 4.4 doubly nested parentheses restating RPM-wT; Section 4.3 '(RPM vs IPL3 Holm p < 0.0001; vs FLAT = 0.270 ...)'. (g) Section 4.3 says that against the PLS truth 'the ordering was unchanged', but FLAT (0.253) and SLOPE-T (0.263) swap ranks relative to the ridge truth (0.266 vs 0.251).
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md: first figure is '**Fig. 2.**'; text citations found: Fig. 2a, 2b, 3, 4, 5, 6 only. Section 4.7 'Supplementary Tables S21–S22'. Section 4.9 text. Section 4.5 last paragraph. Section 4.4. Section 4.3 last paragraph. manuscript/build/supplementary_full.md Table S2 (30 'free' rows vs 38 in tables/T9_theory_validity_full_pool_fit.csv), Table S16 (tables/T19_*.csv has 264 rows), Table S26 (tables/T0_simulation.csv has 108 rows). manuscript/build/build_supplementary.py line 20 (maxrows=60).
issues.corrective_action: Include the workflow figure as Fig. 1 (or renumber), and cite every figure in order. Fix all supplementary cross-references against the final numbering. Remove the 60-row truncation, or split long tables and state explicitly where the full CSVs are. Replace code identifiers with descriptive names and report p-values as 'p < 0.001'. Remove duplicated phrases and nested parentheses. Correct the PLS ordering statement. Have a human author proofread the generated text end to end.

issues.title: 'Pre-registration' is an internal file frozen minutes before the main run; the promised time-stamped log is not in the Supplementary Material; and the Abstract bases its recommendation on post-hoc rules without saying so
issues.description: The manuscript uses 'pre-registered' repeatedly. The design file, however, was frozen internally at 19:10 and the main run started at 19:21, after exploratory runs on one of the evaluation sources (18:52–18:58). It was not deposited on any public registry (OSF, AsPredicted), so referees cannot verify its timing. Section 3.6 says the timing of the post-hoc additions 'is recorded in a time-stamped experiment log (Supplementary Material)', but the Supplementary Material contains no such log. Only Supplementary Note 1 refers to an external file named 'EXPERIMENT_LOG.md'. That log is a hand-edited markdown table with out-of-order entries (14:55 listed before 14:50). Section 3.6 states that RPM-w was specified 'after the main run had been executed', whereas the log shows the main run had only started (19:21) and was completed the next day (14:40). Finally, the Abstract's Significance recommends 'the pilot's cross-validated error, combined with a typical slope and calibrated bands'. Both the slope rule and the calibrated bands were added post hoc and were derived and evaluated on the same 38 tasks, and the Abstract does not say this.
issues.evidence: /home/user/p_c1_8/EXPERIMENT_LOG.md rows 18:52–18:58, 19:10, 19:21, 19:24–19:27, 2026-11-16 14:40, 14:45/14:55/14:50/14:53. manuscript/build/supplementary_full.md Supplementary Note 1 line 'Any later deviation is logged in EXPERIMENT_LOG.md'; no log content elsewhere in the SM (checked the PDF text). manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md Section 3.6 ('specified after the main run had been executed'); Abstract (Significance); Section 5 item 3.
issues.corrective_action: Call the document an 'internally frozen analysis plan' unless a public registration exists, and give its hash or commit time stamp. Include the complete, chronologically ordered decision log as a Supplementary Note. Correct the RPM-w timing wording ('after the main run had started'). In the Abstract, label the slope rule and calibrated bands as post hoc and requiring prospective validation.

issues.title: Key prior art in the target journal and in analytical standards is not cited or compared
issues.description: Beleites et al., 'Sample size planning for classification models', Anal. Chim. Acta 760 (2013) 25–33 (doi:10.1016/j.aca.2012.11.007), is the target journal's own reference paper on learning-curve-based sample-size planning for spectroscopic models, from the same group as the cited Ali et al. [8]. It shows that the uncertainty of a limited test set masks learning curves, which is closely related to this manuscript's conclusion that sample-size forecasting is ill-conditioned. It is not cited. The Introduction also claims that 'current guidance is largely heuristic' without citing the guidance analysts actually follow: ASTM E1655 (minimum numbers of calibration samples relative to model complexity) and ISO 12099 / AACC 39-00 for NIR calibration. ACA asks authors to explain how the proposed methodology compares with previously reported methods, so referees and the editor will expect this positioning.
issues.evidence: grep of manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md and supplementary/*.md: no occurrence of 'Beleites', 'ASTM', 'E1655' or 'ISO 12099'. manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md Section 1 paragraph 1 ('Current guidance is largely heuristic, for example minimum sample numbers expressed relative to model complexity ...' with no citation).
issues.corrective_action: Cite and discuss Beleites et al. (2013) and relate its test-set-size argument to the ill-conditioning result of Section 4.5. Cite ASTM E1655 and ISO 12099, and evaluate the standard minimum-sample rules against the ground-truth curves, e.g. what RMSE the ASTM minimum achieves relative to the asymptote. This is a cheap analysis on existing outputs.

issues.title: 'The theory reproduces the learning curves' is asserted without a reference scale; the omniscient fit is only modestly better than a flat line
issues.description: The headline validation (mean absolute log error 0.113 for ridge) uses a three-parameter fit to the full pool's CV path, with r free. No reference error is given to judge whether 0.113 is good. I recomputed a trivial omniscient reference: a horizontal line at each task's own mean log-RMSE. Its mean absolute log deviation is 0.132 (median 0.119), barely worse than the theory (0.113, median 0.087), and the theory is worse than this constant in 12 of 38 tasks. The theory's error is a median 20% of the total drop of the curve. Fig. 2a shows a systematic optimistic offset at small n for KSSL-MIR:OC. Seven tasks have only two truth points, which makes the curve comparison almost uninformative for them. The κ-collapse statistic (Fig. 2b) is a median over the whole κ range, much of which is the heavily regularised regime where collapse is trivially expected. The visible non-collapse occurs at small κ, the region relevant to extrapolation.
issues.evidence: Recomputed from results/raw/truth_*.npz (0.5·log ridge_mse) and tables/T9_theory_validity_full_pool_fit.csv ('free' rows): mean |deviation from own mean| 0.132 vs theory 0.113; theory worse in 12/38 tasks; median theory error / total curve drop = 0.20. manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md Section 4.1; Fig. 2a (KSSL-MIR:OC dotted curve below markers by about 10–15% at n ≤ 200); Fig. 2b (n = 50–200 curves diverge at κ < 1e-5).
issues.corrective_action: Report reference errors for the validation: a constant, and a 2–3-parameter power law fitted with the same full-pool information. Report the signed bias as a function of n. Restrict the collapse statistic to a window around each n's optimal κ*. Mark tasks with fewer than three truth points and exclude them from the validation summary.

issues.title: RPM forecasts often predict that more samples will increase the error, and the paper's illustrative figure shows RPM worse than the no-improvement rule
issues.description: The RPM forecast is not anchored to the observed pilot CV error. In 34% of RPM forecasts (46% at n0 = 200) the predicted RMSE at the larger calibration size exceeds the pilot's own cross-validated RMSE, i.e. the forecast says that adding samples will make the calibration worse. A practitioner will find such a forecast implausible, and it explains RPM's positive bias. Fig. 5, the only illustration of forecasts, shows exactly this in 2 of its 3 panels: for KSSL-VisNIR:clay and Mango:DM the blue RPM curve lies above the green no-improvement line. Anchoring is applied only in the decision metric (Section 3.4), not in the primary endpoint.
issues.evidence: Recomputed from results/raw_results.csv: share(fc_logrmse > pilot_cv_logrmse) = 0.343 for RPM and 0.338 for RPM-w; by n0: 0.26/0.34/0.39/0.46. figures/Fig3_example_forecasts.png (manuscript Fig. 5); manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md Section 3.4 (anchoring only for decisions).
issues.corrective_action: Evaluate an anchored RPM (forecast gain × pilot CV error, as already used for decisions) as the primary variant, or justify the non-anchored form. Report the share of non-monotone forecasts. Choose a representative illustrative example and disclose how the pilot was selected.

issues.title: Submission package not compliant or not finished: no graphical abstract, placeholders throughout, AI use in the research process not described in Methods, internal workflow jargon in the text and Supplementary Material
issues.description: (a) No graphical abstract file exists, although the project's own journal-selection record lists it among ACA's key requirements. The unused workflow figure would be a natural basis for one. (b) Author names, affiliations, corresponding author, CRediT roles, funding and suggested reviewers are placeholders in the manuscript and cover letter. The AI declaration contains '(Authors: confirm or amend this statement according to the actual use.)'. (c) The declaration says an AI assistant was used for 'literature screening, code development'. Elsevier policy restricts the end-of-manuscript declaration to the writing process and expects AI use in the research process to be described in the Methods, but Section 3.8 does not mention it. (d) Internal project language reaches the reader: 'suggested by the hostile-reviewer check' (Section 3.6; 'hostile-reviewer check' again in Section 4.3). Supplementary Note 2 contains 'Code review (Reviewer-4 round)', 'Robustness results T8', 'Table S0' and 'E7(c,d)', none of which exist in the SM numbering. Supplementary Note 3 contains a 'Topic-selection record' describing topics abandoned as 'crowded in ACA 2026' or for 'generic-DL risk', which is project-management material that does not belong in a journal supplement. (e) The Abstract is 253 words. Check it against the current ACA limit.

Topic-selection record'.
issues.corrective_action: Prepare a graphical abstract. Complete all author, declaration and funding fields. Move the description of AI use in code development and literature screening into Section 3.8. Replace 'hostile-reviewer check' with a neutral description, e.g. 'a simple competitor added after the analysis plan was frozen'. Clean Supplementary Note 2 of internal labels, and delete the topic-selection record from Supplementary Note 3. Trim the Abstract to the journal limit.

issues.title: Length, method proliferation and acronym density make the message hard to extract for an analytical-chemistry readership
issues.description: The 33-page manuscript evaluates 11 forecasting methods (RPM, RPM-w, RPM-T, RPM-wT, SLOPE-T, IPL3, IPL2, EXP3, LOG2, FLAT, DF-OLS), plus 9 ablation variants, a simulation, robustness and shift scenarios, and post-hoc gain, bracket, ratio and conformal analyses. It has 9 main figures, 4 main tables and 35 supplementary tables. The random-matrix theory (Eqs. 2–5, κ, df2, N(κ), alignment exponent) is presented with little intuition for analytical chemists. The practical take-home message (use the pilot CV error, expect a modest gain, do not fit curve shapes) is simple, but it is spread over Sections 4.3–4.10.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md Sections 3.5–3.6 and 4.3–4.9; Table 2 (11 rows); manuscript/Final_Manuscript.pdf (33 pages); manuscript/build/supplementary_full.md Tables S1–S35.
issues.corrective_action: Move RPM-T/RPM-wT, EXP3/LOG2/DF-OLS, the bracket analysis and most ablations to the SM. Keep RPM(-w), IPL3, FLAT and SLOPE-T in the main comparisons. Add an intuitive explanation of κ and of the alignment exponent in spectroscopic terms, e.g. principal-component variance vs analyte information. Aim for about 6–7 main display items.

issues.title: Reference list inconsistently formatted and cites preprints where peer-reviewed versions exist
issues.description: The formatting is inconsistent: full first names in [12]–[14], [18], [19], [24], [25] vs initials elsewhere; '[26] l. E. Frank' (lower-case initial); a stray '*' in the title of [22]; 'Procedures.,' in [37]; hyphenated page ranges; full journal names rather than the abbreviations used in ACA style. Several arXiv citations have peer-reviewed versions: Bordelon et al. [19] (ICML 2020), Jacot et al. [24] (NeurIPS 2020), Wei et al. [25] (ICML 2022) and Adriaensen et al. [12] (NeurIPS 2023).
issues.corrective_action: Apply the ACA reference style consistently, fix the typographical errors and cite the peer-reviewed versions of the preprints.

issues.title: The title suggests a new theory, whereas the risk formula is taken from prior work
issues.description: 'Random-matrix theory of multivariate calibration learning curves' implies a theoretical development. The deterministic-equivalent risk (Eqs. 2–3) is taken from [15,16,18]. The contribution is its empirical validation on spectroscopic data and its use, with limited success, for pilot-based forecasting.
issues.corrective_action: Consider a title such as 'What a small pilot set can and cannot predict about multivariate calibration learning curves: insights from random-matrix theory'.

issues.title: Data-availability statement lacks persistent identifiers, versions and licences, and code deposition is deferred
issues.description: 'OSSL public bucket' and 'Eigenvector Research archive' are given without URL, version or access date. Eigenvector data sets (Diesel, CGL, IDRC-2002) carry their own redistribution terms, while processed copies of the data are shipped in code/data/cache. The code is to be deposited 'upon acceptance' instead of being available to referees through a persistent link. Section 3.8 also contains the odd phrase 'downloads nothing silently'.
issues.corrective_action: Give a URL or DOI, version and licence for every data source. Confirm that the cached files may be redistributed. Deposit the code now (e.g. a Zenodo DOI with a reviewer link) and rephrase the sentence in Section 3.8.

recommendation_rationale: Scope fit is acceptable. A fundamental chemometric study of calibration learning curves on many spectroscopic data sets falls under ACA's 'chemometric techniques and data treatment'. The leakage-controlled benchmark and the demonstration that curve-shape extrapolation is strongly optimistic are useful to the community; the latter is robust across all 9 sources. In its current form, however, the paper is framed as a new forecasting method (RPM) that is not superior to the simplest alternative. RPM is worse than the pilot's own CV error on the soil tasks and at n0 = 200, and it fails the pre-registered decision endpoint. That conflicts with ACA's requirement of clear superiority for new methods and is the main desk-rejection risk (R9-C01-01). The recommended practical rule is post hoc, is itself a power law, and is calibrated mostly on soil libraries (R9-C01-02, -04). The noise-floor explanation of slopes is confounded (R9-C01-03), and the inference ignores clustering by source (R9-C01-05). The package also has technical defects that alone would justify returning it without review (R9-C01-06, -11). None of these is fatal. The data and analyses largely exist, and only the external non-soil validation (R9-C01-04) requires new computation. I would therefore not reject outright. I would return it to the authors for reframing and technical correction before peer review, and then expect a major revision. If the authors keep the 'RPM is better than current practice' framing, my recommendation would be Reject.
